gaps.gap: Status of the Carbon Market Regulations, 2026 (draft with Attorney-General)

gaps.gap: Ghana's first ART TREES (jurisdictional REDD+) credits reported at COP31

gaps.gap: Carbon Market Committee inauguration (due H2 2026)

gaps.how: Check Parliament and partner-government notices.

gaps.gap: Bank carbon-broker licence claim (Access Bank)
gaps.why: Would show private-sector entry, but is unconfirmed.
gaps.how: Find a CMO or regulator notice.
gaps.where: CMO; Bank of Ghana; company press release

gaps.gap: REDD+ benefit-sharing plan and payments to cocoa farmers
gaps.why: $21.8m received in 2025; unclear how much reached communities.
gaps.how: Find the benefit-sharing plan and payment reports.

gaps.gap: Final section of the CMO annual report not yet read
gaps.why: About a fifth of the report (VVB and VCM detail) was not covered.
gaps.how: Read the remaining pages.

gaps.gap: Ministry of Environment, Science and Technology website not reachable
gaps.why: Ministry is the policy lead; need an alternative official source.
gaps.how: Use EPA/CMO and Parliament, or ask the Ministry directly.

gaps.gap: Few peer-reviewed studies of Ghana's Article 6 / ITMO deals
gaps.why: The literature search found only 3 ITMO papers and none on Ghana's transfers: a clear opening for original research.
gaps.how: Make Ghana's ITMO experience a core contribution of your study.

gaps.gap: No independent evidence on whether Ghana's cookstove credits are over-credited
gaps.why: Global evidence shows pervasive over-crediting in cookstove methods (Gill-Wiehl et al., 2024).
gaps.how: Compare project assumptions (fuel use, usage rates) with field evidence.
gaps.where: Project documents on Gold Standard/Verra; household surveys

gaps.gap: Little evidence on who benefits from Article 6 projects in Ghana
gaps.why: Benefit-sharing studies focus on REDD+, not on cookstove, rice or compost ITMO projects.
gaps.how: Interviews and document analysis of revenue flows.

gaps.gap: Gender dimension of carbon projects in Ghana is under-studied
gaps.why: Women manage cooking and fuel, and AWD rice projects report low women's participation.
gaps.how: Gender analysis in interviews; review cooking-fuel health studies.

gaps.gap: No studies on AWD rice or compost ITMO projects in Ghana
gaps.why: These are new Article 6 project types with farmer-payment challenges.
gaps.how: Case study of UNDP-supported projects.

gaps.gap: Weak verification capacity (VVB average 2.25/5) not analysed in literature
gaps.why: Credit quality depends on verification.
gaps.how: Interview CMO and developers on MRV and verifiers.

gaps.gap: Effect of credit sales on Ghana's own NDC ambition
gaps.why: Selling too many credits could make Ghana's targets harder to meet.
gaps.how: Compare authorised volumes with NDC conditional/unconditional targets.

dirs.t: Who benefits from Ghana's ITMO deals?
dirs.q: How is revenue from Ghana's Article 6 transfers shared between government, developers and households, and do benefits reach women and the poor?
dirs.why: First-mover case in Africa; benefit sharing is the biggest open question and is not yet studied for ITMO projects.
dirs.m: Document analysis; key-informant interviews; household survey in project areas
dirs.data: CMO reports; Act 1124; project documents; interviews
dirs.lit: Atiawin & Abubakar (2026) on Ghana's carbon credit regulation; Kandala (2026) on carbon rights and benefit sharing

dirs.q: Do the assumptions behind Ghana's cookstove credits match real fuel use and stove adoption?
dirs.why: Cookstoves are 58% of the pipeline and most transfers; global studies show pervasive over-crediting.
dirs.m: Compare project design documents with field data; stove-use and fuel surveys
dirs.data: Gold Standard/Verra project files; CMO; household data
dirs.lit: Gill-Wiehl et al. (2024), Nature Sustainability; Perros et al. (2026) on cookstove and biogas credits

dirs.q: How does Ghana's institutional sequencing of carbon-market rules compare with Kenya and Nigeria, and what explains the differences?
dirs.why: Ghana is presented as a model for Africa; comparative evidence is new and policy-relevant.
dirs.m: Comparative policy analysis; legal review; expert interviews
dirs.data: National laws; UNEP-CCC Article 6 Pipeline; ACMI
dirs.lit: Okoh et al. (2026) comparative study of Ghana, Kenya and Nigeria; Clark (2025) on sovereign carbon markets

dirs.t: From REDD+ payments to jurisdictional credits
dirs.q: How have communities in Ghana's cocoa landscapes experienced REDD+ results-based payments, and what changes with ART TREES credits?
dirs.why: $21.8m received in 2025 and first ART TREES credits reported; justice concerns raised in recent studies.
dirs.m: Interviews in Hotspot Intervention Areas; review of benefit-sharing plan
dirs.data: Forestry Commission; FCPF reports; ART registry
dirs.lit: Nyarko & Ashiagbor (2025); 2026 Forest Policy and Economics papers on REDD+ safeguards and community apathy in Ghana

dirs.q: How do carbon-financed cookstove projects affect women's time, health and decision-making in Ghana?
dirs.why: Women manage cooking; links carbon markets to health and gender equity.
dirs.m: Mixed methods: household survey and focus groups
dirs.data: PubMed health studies; project data; GSS
dirs.lit: Okyere et al. (2024) gendered health effects of cooking fuels in southern Ghana; Adarkwa et al. (2024) cooking smoke and anaemia

dirs.t: New project types: rice (AWD) and compost
dirs.q: What drives smallholder adoption of AWD rice and composting under Article 6, and how well do ITMO payments work for farmers?
dirs.why: Novel project types with no published studies; CMO reports payment-understanding and water challenges.
dirs.m: Case study; farmer interviews; payment-system analysis
dirs.lit: Few direct studies: use CMO report plus agricultural carbon-credit literature in the Literature tab

dirs.q: Why do verification bodies perform poorly in Ghana, and could digital MRV improve credit quality?
dirs.why: VVB average 2.25/5 is a striking official finding; affects credibility.
dirs.m: Interviews with CMO, VVBs and developers; review of digital MRV tools
dirs.data: CMO report; ICVCM; World Bank Climate Warehouse
dirs.lit: Carbon removal and technology theme in the Literature tab (MRV, remote sensing)

dirs.t: Credit sales and Ghana's NDC ambition
dirs.q: Does authorising credits for export put Ghana's own NDC targets at risk?
dirs.why: Core Article 6 policy dilemma; Ghana has authorised 53% of its 24 Mt Article 6 budget.
dirs.m: Quantitative comparison of authorised volumes with NDC targets
dirs.lit: Hörnsten (2026) on trading and ambition; Article 6 theme in the Literature tab

dirs.q: How transparent are the prices and revenues of Ghana's bilateral ITMO deals?
dirs.why: Only a $66m estimate is public; transparency matters for public trust.
dirs.m: Document analysis; interviews; comparison with other countries' deals
dirs.lit: Voluntary market and integrity theme in the Literature tab

dirs.q: What role do Ghanaian banks, brokers and developers play in the carbon market?
dirs.why: Supports Step 6; private actors are emerging but under-studied.
dirs.data: Ghana Carbon Registry; company disclosures; B&FT
dirs.lit: Osman et al. (2026) on sovereign green bonds in Ghana

dirs.q: Could Ghana's mangroves generate credible blue-carbon credits?
dirs.why: Emerging frontier with a World Bank readiness assessment.
dirs.lit: World Bank (2024) Ghana: A Blue Carbon Readiness Assessment

dirs.q: How would a carbon tax or levy affect Ghanaian households?
dirs.why: Useful if Ghana moves from crediting to pricing.
dirs.lit: 2025 Environment and Development Economics paper on carbon pricing impacts in Ghana and Nigeria

messages: Progress, not perfection: one paper read today is one more than yesterday.
Ghana is writing Africa's carbon-market playbook, and you are documenting it as it happens.
Protect your first 25 minutes: phone in another room, one tab open.
Every gap you close is a question few people have answered yet.
Small daily steps compound: 25 minutes a day is over 150 hours a year.
Your research can shape how carbon money reaches farmers and women. That matters.
Start with the hardest task while your energy is highest.
Distracted? Write the distraction down, then return to work. Deal with it later.
Experts were once beginners who did not quit.
Read with one question in mind: what does this mean for Ghana?
A first draft only needs to exist. Polish it later.
Celebrate small wins: tick it off, log it, earn the XP.
Little by little, the bird builds its nest. (Proverb)
Sankofa: go back for what you have forgotten. Review yesterday's notes before starting.
One sharp question beats ten vague ones. Sharpen today's question.
If you can explain it simply, you understand it. Explain Article 6 to a friend today.
Check the source before you trust the number.
Rest is part of the work. Take a real break after four focus sessions.
Your future self will thank you for today's notes.
Consistency beats intensity. Show up again tomorrow.
Ask one expert one question this week. Networks grow one conversation at a time.
Turn what you learn into something you can share: a post, a brief, a slide.
Stuck? Shrink the task: open the file, read one page, write one sentence.
Be curious, not just busy. What surprised you today?
What gets tracked gets improved. Log today's focus sessions.
One new skill a month adds up to twelve in a year.
You are building expertise that few people in Africa have yet.
Clear desk, clear mind, clear question.
End the day by writing tomorrow's first task.
Discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want now.
